analysis.one_liner: Forces federal agencies through slower, cost-first procedures before issuing major regulations.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 250-175 on January 13, 2015, with 242 of 242 voting Republicans in favor, but the Senate never voted and it died when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the procedures every federal agency must follow before issuing a major rule. Agencies would have to publish an advance notice and gather evidence first, hold trial-style hearings where regulated companies can cross-examine government witnesses before the costliest rules, and by default adopt the cheapest option that meets the law's goals. Courts would also be barred from deferring to an agency's own interpretations and cost analyses, making it much easier to challenge rules in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses regulated by federal rules — in energy, manufacturing, chemicals, finance, and beyond — would gain powerful new tools to delay, weaken, or kill costly rules: advance-notice requirements, cross-examination hearings, a legal mandate that agencies pick the least costly rule, and expanded court challenges. The White House budget office (OIRA) would also gain new authority over how agencies analyze and issue rules.

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would generally have to adopt the least costly rule that meets statutory objectives, choosing a costlier rule only if its extra benefits justify the extra costs and the agency explains why based on public health, safety, or welfare [S4].

Before adopting any rule with an estimated $1 billion or more in annual economic costs, agencies would have to hold a formal hearing with a reasonable opportunity for cross-examination of the evidence, and would have to grant hearings on any major rule unless a hearing clearly would not help [S4, S3].
Courts would be barred from deferring to an agency's interpretation of a rule, its cost-benefit determinations that don't follow OIRA guidelines, its interim rules, or its guidance documents [S4].

Any interested person could petition for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule, could seek a hearing challenging the evidence behind a proposed rule, and could get immediate judicial review of interim rules issued without full notice [S4, S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who depend on federal protections would bear the cost: workplace safety, clean air and water, food safety, consumer finance, and other rules would take longer, cost more to produce, and be far easier to stall in litigation. The bill's default of the 'least costly' rule could force agencies to accept weaker protections even when a stronger rule's benefits clearly exceed its costs.

drawbacks.text: The default rule that agencies must pick the least costly option could require weaker health, safety, and environmental protections even where the benefits of a stronger rule plainly justify its costs [S4].

Trial-like hearings with cross-examination before major rules could stall urgent rulemaking for months or years, since agencies would need to produce evidence and defend it against cross-examination before acting [S4].

Supporters argue current rulemaking is already slow and costly and that compliance burdens fall heavily on small businesses; provisions requiring agencies to publish the evidence they rely on and to consider lower-cost alternatives have transparency value in themselves [S2, S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is framed as making regulation more evidence-based and transparent, and some provisions — public dockets, reasoned analysis, a right to petition — have genuine value. But its core mechanics point one way: a legal default toward the cheapest rule, adversarial hearings, and narrower court deference would make any significant protective rule dramatically slower and more vulnerable to challenge. For ordinary people, the likely trade is modest procedural transparency in exchange for substantially weaker and slower protections, which is a poor bargain.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House 250-175 in January 2015, was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and never got a Senate vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 7, 2015, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and immediately fast-tracked: the Rules Committee structured floor debate under a rule that waived points of order and allowed only pre-printed amendments [S6].

On January 13, 2015, the House rejected a Democratic motion to recommit that would have added an exemption for rules that prevent terrorism and crime, protect workers' wages, save tax dollars, assist small business, or prevent discrimination, by a recorded vote of 180-245, with all 243 voting Republicans opposed [S7, S6].
The House passed the bill 250-175 the same day: 242 of 245 Republicans voted yes and none voted no, while 8 of 188 Democrats voted yes and 175 voted no [S8].

The Senate received the bill on January 16, 2015 and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, where no further action was taken; the Congress ended January 3, 2017 without a Senate vote [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, federal agencies kept the existing rulemaking process, and the protections issued under it — on worker safety, wages, air and water quality, and consumer finance — could continue to be written without the bill's least-cost mandate and hearing requirements. The regulated industries that sought the added procedural shields did not get them; the bill's House passage alone changed no law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, consumers, and the rules that protect them

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through the House, which passed it 13 days after introduction.

for.name: 242 of 245 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, supplying all but 8 of the 250 votes for it.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the rule (H. Res. 27) that brought the bill straight to the floor, waived points of order, and limited amendments to those printed in the report.

against.name: Rep. Kathleen Rice
against.what_they_did: Offered a motion to recommit instructing the committee to exempt rules that prevent terrorism and crime, protect workers' wages, save tax dollars, assist small business, or prevent discrimination; it failed 180-245.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 16, 2015 and never acted on it; it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Consumer, labor, and environmental advocacy groups
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the bill as a mechanism to delay or weaken health, safety, wage, and environmental regulations.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was nearly a party-line split: 242 of 245 Republicans voted yes and none voted no, while 175 of 188 Democrats voted no, with 8 Democrats crossing over; the motion to recommit split the other way, with all 180 yes votes from Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would give these companies advance notice, cross-examination hearings, a least-cost default, and expanded court review — tools to delay or dilute costly rules. What the industries save in compliance, the public gives up in slower or weaker health, safety, wage, and environmental protections.

industries.industry: Regulatory litigation bar and consulting firms
industries.note: Expanded rights to petition for hearings, challenge evidence under the Information Quality Act, and seek immediate judicial review would create years of additional litigation work for firms that contest federal rules.
